summary: Daniel receives another vision during Belshazzar’s reign, this time seeing a two-horned ram defeated by a swift male goat whose great horn breaks and is replaced by four horns. From one horn comes a smaller horn that attacks the sanctuary, the continual burnt offering, and the holy people, until a timed cleansing is announced. Gabriel then explains the ram as Media and Persia, the goat as Greece, and a later fierce king whose power will end without human hands.
whyItMatters: This chapter begins Daniel’s Hebrew vision section and gives unusually direct identifications for some of its symbols. It narrows the book’s empire visions toward attacks on worship, truth, and the holy people, while still leaving Daniel sick and without full understanding.

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel’s first-person voice; the book does not name a final editor. Traditional readers identify Daniel as author, while most critical scholarship sees a second-century BC final composition using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The story is set in the sixth-century BC Babylonian court period, in the third year of Belshazzar. Many scholars date the book’s final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, during the Antiochus IV crisis; traditional readings understand the visions as earlier predictive prophecy.
context.setting: Daniel sees the vision in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam, by the river Ulai, while the book’s larger setting moves between Babylonian and Persian courts and visions of later empires.
context.literaryForm: Apocalyptic vision with symbolic animals, horns, heavenly speakers, a numbered period, and angelic interpretation.

outline.heading: The Vision Begins at Susa
outline.note: Daniel dates the vision to Belshazzar’s reign and locates himself in the vision at Susa by the Ulai.

outline.heading: The Ram and the Goat
outline.note: A powerful two-horned ram is overthrown by a male goat; the goat’s great horn breaks and four horns arise in its place.

outline.heading: The Little Horn Attacks Worship
outline.note: A little horn grows great, casts down heavenly imagery, removes the continual burnt offering, and casts truth to the ground.

outline.heading: How Long?
outline.note: Holy ones ask how long the trampling will last, and the answer gives two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings before the sanctuary is cleansed.

outline.heading: Gabriel Is Told to Explain
outline.note: Daniel seeks understanding, is frightened and overcome, and Gabriel says the vision belongs to the time of the end.

outline.heading: The Symbols Named
outline.note: Gabriel identifies the ram with Media and Persia, the goat with Greece, the great horn as the first king, and the four horns as four lesser kingdoms.

outline.heading: A Fierce King and Daniel’s Aftermath
outline.note: Gabriel describes a destructive king who prospers, deceives, attacks holy people, and is broken without human hands; Daniel is sick, resumes the king’s business, and remains bewildered.

keyVerses.text: He said to me, “To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.”
keyVerses.why: This gives the vision’s answer to the question of duration, while not explaining every detail of how the number should be counted.

keyVerses.text: The ram which you saw, that had the two horns, they are the kings of Media and Persia.
keyVerses.why: The chapter itself identifies one of its major symbols, so readers do not have to guess at this point.

keyVerses.text: The rough male goat is the king of Greece. The great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
keyVerses.why: This is the second major built-in interpretation, naming Greece and the first king represented by the great horn.

keyVerses.text: I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick for some days. Then I rose up and did the king’s business. I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it.
keyVerses.why: The ending shows that even after explanation, the vision overwhelms Daniel and remains partly beyond ordinary understanding.

questions.question: Where does this vision happen?
questions.answer: Daniel says the vision appeared in the third year of King Belshazzar. In the vision he is in the citadel of Susa, in Elam, by the river Ulai. The chapter presents this as visionary location rather than a travel report explained in ordinary narrative detail.

questions.question: What do the ram and male goat stand for?
questions.answer: The chapter gives its own explanation. Gabriel says the ram with two horns represents the kings of Media and Persia, and the rough male goat represents the king of Greece. The great horn is identified as the first king, while the four horns that follow are four kingdoms from the same nation but with less power.

questions.question: Why are horns so important in the vision?
questions.answer: In this chapter horns mark political power within the symbolic animals. The ram’s two horns are later interpreted as Media and Persia, the goat’s great horn as a first Greek king, and the four later horns as four kingdoms. The chapter does not define every symbolic detail, but it clearly uses horns to picture rulers or kingdoms.

questions.question: Who is the little horn?
questions.answer: The chapter describes the little horn as growing exceedingly great, attacking the sanctuary and the holy people, and later as a fierce king who prospers through destructive power and deceit. The visions reach toward Antiochus IV Epiphanes and his violent policies against Jewish worship. Readers differ on whether the chapter is only about that Antiochene crisis or also establishes a wider pattern of arrogant persecuting power.

questions.question: What is the continual burnt offering?
questions.answer: The chapter names the continual burnt offering as something taken away and connected with the sanctuary’s being trampled. It does not pause to describe the ritual system in detail. For a first reading, the important point inside this chapter is that regular worship is interrupted as part of the horn’s attack.

questions.question: What does “two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase answers the question, “How long,” and says the sanctuary will be cleansed after that period. Interpreters debate whether the phrase counts full days, evening and morning offerings, or symbolic time within the crisis described by the vision. The chapter itself gives the number and the outcome, but does not supply a calendar conversion.

questions.question: What does “the time of the end” mean here?
questions.answer: Gabriel says the vision belongs to the time of the end and to the appointed time of the end. In this chapter, that language is tied to the latter time of the indignation and to the later phase of the kingdoms being described. Readers differ on how far beyond the Antiochene crisis the phrase should be extended, so it is safest to start with the chapter’s own sequence before making larger claims.

questions.question: Why does Daniel become sick if Gabriel explains the vision?
questions.answer: The explanation does not make the vision easy to bear. Daniel is frightened, falls on his face, enters a deep sleep, and later faints and is sick for some days. The chapter portrays revelation as overwhelming and only partly understood by Daniel.

questions.question: Does the chapter say the violent king wins?
questions.answer: The king prospers for a time and destroys many, including the mighty ones and the holy people. Yet the explanation also says he will stand against the prince of princes and be broken without human hands. The chapter therefore depicts severe temporary success, but not final control.

glossary.def: The form in which Daniel sees symbolic events and then receives an explanation; the word appears repeatedly through the chapter.
The two-horned animal Daniel sees pushing in several directions; Gabriel identifies it as the kings of Media and Persia.
The animal from the west that defeats the ram; Gabriel identifies it with the king of Greece.
A repeated image for power in the vision, used for the ram, the goat’s first king, later kingdoms, and the little horn.
The holy place affected by the horn’s attack and later said to be cleansed.
The named figure commanded to make Daniel understand the vision.
